depth/image: A color image has three channels, red, green and blue, each a grid of pixels. Channels first, as PyTorch writes it, its shape is C by H by W: channels, height and width. Here, three by thirty two by thirty two.
depth/filter: A filter always has the full depth of its input. Here it is three by three by three: a three by three patch in every channel, twenty seven weights.
depth/one: At each position it multiplies all twenty seven pairs and adds them up, giving one number. Not one per color: one.
depth/map: Slid over every position where it fits, those numbers fill one thirty by thirty map: a single output channel.
many/k: A layer has many filters, K of them, each with its own weights, each looking for its own pattern. Here, eight.
many/stack: Each filter makes its own map, and the maps stack up as the output's channels. Eight filters, eight channels: eight by thirty by thirty.
many/shape: So the output's depth is the number of filters. Its height and width are how many places the filter fits, as before: thirty two minus three plus one.
many/next: The next layer sees an input eight channels deep, so each of its filters is eight deep: eight by three by three, depth first.
layer/args: In PyTorch, n n dot conv two d, of three, eight, kernel size five builds a layer. Its numbers come in order: three channels in, eight channels out, then the kernel size, five. Kernel is another word for filter.
layer/filters: Eight channels out means eight filters: K is eight. Three channels in means each filter is three deep: three by five by five, depth first. Seventy five weights each.
layer/weight: PyTorch stacks the eight filters along a new first axis, so the weight has shape eight, three, five, five: filters, depth, height and width. Out comes first, then in.
layer/out: Run it on an image of shape three by thirty two by thirty two. Eight filters make eight channels, and a five wide filter fits thirty two minus five plus one, twenty eight places, down and across: eight by twenty eight by twenty eight.
